title: My childhood dream MMORPG is available: Halvel.com
author: Ok-Cook-7365
selftext:
Game is a fully featured MMORPG with music, follower systems and gameplay. Everything is available to play for free. This is about 8 months of game development. 

Games cross platform as well.

comments.author: Ok-Cook-7365
comments.body:
Models used were fable 5, opus 4.8, at one point some GLM 5.1, opus 5 which sucked, and at times Qwen 3.8 27B on my own hardware at home but that proved less fruitful.

I’d say now the game feels like it has enough there for me to have fun and scratch my MMORPG itch. And anyone can play which is fun.

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body: u/Ok-Cook-7365 please add some details about how you used AI to develop this. Saying you used AI isn't enough on its own. We're looking for the actual dev details. Rule 4 asks promotional posts to contribute by talking about the process and the actual development. We're trying to keep the sub from filling up with low quality game posts. If this doesn't get updated, it may be removed.

comments.author: Xinnobun
comments.body: The problem with MMORPGs is it needs people to keep it alive. Without people, it starts dying then becomes a shell of its former glory. And with the release of hundreds of other MMORPGs, the player base is scattered.

replies.author: civil_politician
replies.body:
I played wow for a decade as a solo game basically, with “groups” of strangers for the dungeons and raids that were probably the worst part of the whole experience. 

If you did AI party it really wouldn’t be that different. Ideally a lot of people play but I still think these exercises are worthwhile.

replies.author: Xinnobun
replies.body:
The whole point of the MMO genre and experience is to live in a massive world shared with other people. If I wanted to do an AI party, I would play a single player game. If I want to play an MMORPG, I plan on playing it to experience it with others. If theres no one, then its a dead game and a hard pass. 

The point I'm trying to make is calling it an MMORPG requires a lot more effort to keep it alive and running. Facebook spent $80 billion trying to build and maintain Metaverse, but it died anyway due to failed population. Creating a successful game as solodev is tough, creating a successful MMORPG game as solodev is even tougher.

replies.author: tj0120
replies.body: You're upset he said MMORPG instead of MORPG or 'online co-op'. Ok. Note taken.

replies.author: Xinnobun
replies.body: I'm pointing out that he's setting the bar significantly higher for himself right from the start. There's nothing to be upset about.

replies.author: Ok-Cook-7365
replies.body: I basically built an entire feature set around that AI party system. You could actually have your AI followers go and camp an area.

replies.author: Moresson
replies.body: Can’t become a shell of its former glory if it was always just a shell *taps head*

comments.author: ItsDumi
comments.body: It looks just like everyone else's ai dream mmorpg, nice

comments.author: ChadSexman
comments.body:
You’ve got to spend some time to de-slop the page dude.

“Quests that carry you” wtf does that mean?

With respect, if you’re not going to spend 5 minutes writing your own tag lines then I think it will be a hard sell to convince people to play.

And ditch that cinzel font, it’s everywhere.

replies.author: Ok-Cook-7365
replies.body:
Hey I appreciate the feedback! I’ll take it. 

Maybe there’s some trade offs for doing a few things by hand but by and large it’s been really nice shipping entire sections of the game maybe 4-10 updates at a time when I worked on this, all at once without lifting a finger.

Wow, RuneScape, etc. would do a patch Tuesday. Imagine logging in each day and seeing new content. That is basically where I was before I paused development. Now I’m sort of in this limbo where I’m trying building a few other projects.

comments.author: Sirramza
comments.body: hey, there is some cool stuff in there, why did you choose to say "fk it" and release it now for free?

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: What makes this your dream MMO that every other MMO that was made by a hundreds professional devs over the past 20 years didn't give you? Everyone is always like "This is a game I dreamt about since I was a kid" and it's the most generic version of some well-tread genre

replies.author: Ok-Cook-7365
replies.body:
Quite a lot that I don’t write out here I suppose:

 \- follower system where you recruit NPCs and gear them up like you would your own character  
 \- housing and fortress system that at end game, you can level up, have your followers defend it and it becomes like Rust meets RTS. Combined with gearing your followers it’s really endless.  
 \- world fold system: you basically have heroic and legendary versions of the world and levels. Like a zone more than another one? Stay and level in it and get equivalent rewards  
 \- gear improvement system: like a piece of gear? Keep leveling it up and basically take other pieces of equipment and combine them into the gear you like  
 \- collection systems and all the obvious stuff as usual  
 \- king over a zone: you can in some zones be the king of that zone by killing the NPC or player king. You then get taxes from anything in that area.

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body: Honestly it looks like it should be playable in browser

replies.author: Ok-Cook-7365
replies.body:
It was but the performance in a browser is severely limited. I have integration with AMD FSR and Nvidia in game to make use of the graphics cards features.

Some of the gameplay is really visually intensive especially after I made it so large sections of the world are progressively loaded by just walking.

comments.author: challengethegods
comments.body:
it's very cool, but has way too much ephemeral fluffy-text compared to actual RPG stats and effect descriptions. I don't want to know that "blows land lighter" I want to know WTF the skill actually does.  
  
some clunkyness, beta vibe, lack of polish/optimization, etc. is probably fine, but quite a lot of it here.   
for example the early area as a ninja/shade was full of friction. If I wasn't such a pro gamer elite megamind I'd probably just die to the noob wisp over and over and give up, but even killing all of those I get a quest reward and then it says "ninja can't use that". More accurately, it gives some generic error and I dig deeper to find the reason I can't use it, since the icons/tooltips weren't intuitive enough to handle it on their own. If the quest rewards are setup for people to choose their rewards among multiple options they cannot even use, the icons/tooltips need to visibly invalidate the wrong choices, and more likely they need to offer only valid options in the early areas. as a dev you will accumulate blindness to how a new player views things, but emulating new player experience can be done with some certain mindset of skipping random steps you normally expect to take. 

Even something as simple as tooltips being inconsistent or too transparent can add to whatever existing frustrations were already there, since it adds another cost to parsing the text (ex: spellbook tooltips are abnormally wide, quest reward tooltips have stuff visible behind them)  


glaring LLM descriptions/explanations all over the place are heavily taxing here.  
I'm as pro-AI as anyone can be, but you have to understand the LLMs are running blind and cannot play the games they are being asked to work on. In most cases they cannot even see the full context of what they are working on or it becomes summarized, so they default into this safely-vague way of talking about everything and pad out all kinds of random flavor text, and stuff mini-tutorials all over the UI.   
  
in my opinion, you should double down on displaying raw mechanics/stats/effects/etc, color code whatever you can, put as much emphasis on the RPG elements as possible, and consider descriptions as basically optional flavor text.  personally I play RPGs to theorycraft and min/max, so having stats/effects visible at a glance rather than buried in thematic poetry or w/e is more ideal. As an example, even the race selection has all kinds of fluffy padding around +/-5% movespeed, and class select gives almost nothing to work with in terms of mechanics. I basically have to create the character based on tone of language, which is not the RPG appeal I think. I found myself using the wiki on the site just to mitigate the in-game veil. LLMs alone cannot solve this because they tend to have no idea what is relevant information and are just as likely to inform you that "right click to loot" is an option after every battle, because who knows, maybe people that play games need to know that? You have to chill out the tutorial-spam a little, even if it helps 'sometimes'.  


what you have here is a good foundation in need of refinement.   
There's tons of settings and features and cool stuff buried beneath a rather crude entry. I'm not a fan of world of warcraft and think it's slow and tedious and boring, but I can respect the scale of trying to aim in that direction, it's not like what you're attempting here is easy. Most likely there's also no quick way to rush across testing and polishing everything, you just have to make new characters and nitpick every point of friction. 

hopefully this helps, even if it sounds like I'm just complaining about random things.  
tbc, I complain about my own projects 10x more than this all day every day, which is like my entire mode of operation for iterating what to work on next, so no need to feel bad about it or anything like that. You can pick/choose which parts seem like they are worth caring about from this, using it as an alternate perspective.
